Distribution of flexibility potential across the customer base for each end use (2030 low price forecast - Full tariff design is shown) 4.4 End uses and enabling technologies 4.4.1 End uses modeled in this study Our results show that, across all price scenarios, metrics, and types of potential, EVs and space cooling (particularly in the residential sector) are the primary contributors to price response potential. These end uses make up 75-80% of the 2030 technical and economic price response potential across all metrics and tariff design scenarios. Pool pumps contribute 8-13%, crop irrigation 6-9%, and residential water heating 3-6%. Space heating drove the smallest contribution, particularly in the effective shed metric, but did constitute 1-2% of the savings metrics. These findings are perhaps unsurprising, but reinforce the need for continued development of flexibility offerings for these end uses. This study considered flexibility of the entirety of load at the end use level20, without consideration for what specific equipment may be required to enable price response. For example, smart thermostats that enable price response of space cooling loads may not be compatible with window units or mini splits that aren’t controlled by a typical thermostat set up. 20 In past studies, “pumping” was an end use present in agriculture and industrial sectors; in this study, we did not model the complete flexibility of pumping in the ag sector, but instead limited it to sites that seemed to be growing irrigated crops per their NAICS code. Hence the “crop irrigation” end use term. 59 Additionally, most flexibility technologies targeting water heating are focused on heat pump water heaters and may not be applicable to electric resistance heaters. It should also be noted that the underlying load model used in this study was developed in 2021 and therefore forecasts around electrification of space and water heating, and adoption of electric vehicles, may not be aligned with current expectations. All of these factors could impact the total price response potential of these end uses. 4.4.2 Additional end use loads This study covers a subset of potentially flexible end use loads, for which the approximate load response mechanism and dispatch strategy could be modeled. Of the electricity demand that occurs in the net peak load hour, 40% is included in this study’s analysis. This is shown in hour 18 of the left panel of Figure 40. An additional 20% of the coincident peak load comes from other end uses that could likely be price responsive (refrigeration, residential appliances, commercial and medium-heavy duty EVs, and industrial process loads).
